subject: Business
title: When to Delegate vs. Decide Yourself
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: When to Delegate vs. Decide Yourself.

hook.text: A founder reviews every hire, every expense, every design. The company has 200 employees. They become the bottleneck.

buildup.text: Delegation isn't abdication. It's assigning the right decisions to the people closest to the information.

discovery.text: Amazon's principle: decisions should be made by the person with the most relevant context, not the highest title.

twist.text: Leaders who can't delegate either don't trust their team or haven't built one worth trusting.

climax.text: Decide yourself when the stakes are existential and irreversible. Delegate everything else.

punchline.text: A leader who decides everything decides nothing well.

quiz.question: When should a leader make decisions themselves instead of delegating?
options: When the stakes are existential and the decision is irreversible

details.summary: Effective delegation requires knowing which decisions to keep and which to push down. Leaders should retain decisions that are irreversible, organization-defining, or uniquely informed by their position, while delegating everything else to build team capability and increase organizational speed.
details.whyItMatters: Leaders who cannot delegate become bottlenecks that slow their organization. Leaders who delegate everything lose oversight of critical decisions. The art is knowing which category each decision falls into and acting accordingly.
takeaways: Delegate reversible decisions to build team capability and increase speed
Retain irreversible and organization-defining decisions that require your judgment
Over-centralizing decisions creates bottlenecks; over-delegating loses strategic control

faq.question: What types of decisions should leaders always keep for themselves?
faq.answer: Decisions that are irreversible or very costly to reverse. Strategic direction changes affecting the entire organization. Decisions requiring information only the leader possesses. Situations where the leader's personal authority or relationships are needed. Ethical matters setting precedent.

faq.question: How do you delegate effectively without micromanaging?
faq.answer: Clearly define the desired outcome, constraints, and decision authority. Provide necessary context and resources. Set check-in points for updates without requiring approval. Accept that the approach may differ from how you would have done it. Evaluate results, not methods.
